content: Poliomyelitis, commonly referred to as polio or infantile paralysis, is an acute viral infection that spreads primarily through the fecal-oral route. The term poliomyelitis originates from the Greek words polio, meaning grey, and myelon, referring to the spinal cord, with the suffix -itis indicating inflammation. While approximately 90% of polio infections are asymptomatic, the virus can cause a spectrum of symptoms if it enters the bloodstream. In less than 1% of cases, the virus invades the central nervous system, targeting and destroying motor neurons. This can result in muscle weakness and acute flaccid paralysis. The type of paralysis depends on the specific nerves affected. Spinal polio, the most common form, is characterized by asymmetric paralysis, often involving the legs. Bulbar polio affects muscles controlled by cranial nerves, while bulbospinal polio is a combination of both spinal and bulbar paralysis. Poliomyelitis was first identified as a distinct disease by Jakob Heine in 1840, and its causative agent, the poliovirus, was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1908. Although major epidemics were not documented before the 20th century, polio became one of the most feared childhood diseases during that time, particularly in the United States. Historically, polio existed as an endemic pathogen for thousands of years, but large-scale epidemics began in the 1880s in Europe and later spread to the United States. By the early 20th century, polio epidemics became a regular occurrence, especially in urban areas during summer months. These outbreaks, which left thousands paralyzed, spurred the development of vaccines. Jonas Salk developed the first polio vaccine in 1952, followed by Albert Sabin's oral vaccine in 1962. These vaccines dramatically reduced the global incidence of polio, from hundreds of thousands of cases annually to just a few thousand. Ongoing vaccination campaigns led by organizations such as the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and Rotary International aim to achieve global eradication of the disease. The term poliomyelitis encompasses the disease caused by any of the three serotypes of poliovirus. Polio infections are classified into two main patterns: a minor illness that does not involve the central nervous system (abortive poliomyelitis) and a major illness that does involve the CNS, which can be either paralytic or non-paralytic. Poliovirus is transmitted through the fecal-oral or oral route. The virus initially infects the oropharynx and gastrointestinal tract, where it replicates for about a week before penetrating the intestinal lining. Once in the bloodstream, the virus causes viremia, spreading throughout the body. In rare cases, the viremia progresses, allowing the virus to invade the central nervous system and trigger a localized inflammatory response. Polio is caused by the poliovirus, a highly infectious agent that invades the nervous system. The virus is small (27–30 nm), non-enveloped, and contains a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome approximately 7,500 nucleotides in length. Transmission occurs primarily through the fecal-oral route, although oral-oral transmission may also occur in some cases. Due to extensive eradication efforts, the number of countries where polio remains a risk has significantly decreased. The last documented case of wild poliovirus-associated paralysis in a U.S. resident occurred in 1986 in a vaccinated adult who had traveled to South and Southeast Asia. In 2005, an unvaccinated U.S. adult contracted vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis after contact with an infant recently vaccinated with the oral polio vaccine. Poliovirus is highly contagious, with nearly 100% seroconversion rates among susceptible household contacts of infected children and over 90% among susceptible adult contacts. Infected individuals are most contagious from 7 to 10 days before and after symptom onset, although the virus can be shed in stool for 3 to 6 weeks. In many cases, poliomyelitis results in only temporary paralysis. However, 25%–40% of individuals who experienced paralytic polio during childhood may develop post-polio syndrome 30–40 years later. This condition is characterized by new muscle pain, worsening weakness, or the development of new paralysis. Patients with abortive polio infections typically recover completely. In cases involving aseptic meningitis, symptoms usually resolve within 2 to 10 days, followed by full recovery. The clinical presentation of poliovirus infection varies widely, ranging from asymptomatic cases to severe manifestations such as acute flaccid paralysis, quadriplegia, respiratory failure, and, in rare instances, death. Laboratory diagnosis is typically based on the isolation of poliovirus from stool or pharyngeal samples. The presence of neutralizing antibodies to poliovirus in the blood can also confirm infection. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, obtained via lumbar puncture, often reveals elevated white blood cell counts (primarily lymphocytes) and mildly increased protein levels. Detection of poliovirus in the CSF is diagnostic of paralytic polio but is rarely observed. There is no specific antiviral treatment for poliomyelitis. Two vaccines are used globally to prevent polio: the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) and the oral polio vaccine (OPV). Both vaccines are highly effective in inducing immunity and preventing person-to-person transmission of wild poliovirus. By achieving herd immunity, these vaccines protect both vaccinated individuals and the broader community.
